source: Alaboudi and LaToza (2020) Using Hypotheses as a Debugging Aid
finding: Controlled study with three conditions (control, two fault locations, two potential hypotheses). Potential hypotheses raised fix success. Fault locations did not.
numbers: 25 recruited, 5 used as pilot, 20 analysed; 3 tasks; 60 sessions. Potential hypotheses: about 6 times more likely to fix (p=0.0388). Success by task in that condition: 2/6, 4/6, 7/8. Tasks 1 and 2 had about 55% success overall, task 3 about 90%.
limits: Small N. Regression with several control variables. p just under .05, so the size of the effect is fragile. Web tasks (JavaScript, React, CSS) taken from Stack Overflow questions.
agent_relevance: Read the six-fold gain as a direction (hypotheses beat locations), not as a size to plan around.

source: Alaboudi and LaToza (2020) Using Hypotheses as a Debugging Aid
finding: The supplied potential hypotheses were generalised, written as a tool might write them. Each pair held one correct and one incorrect hypothesis, with a how-to-test step.
numbers: Two hypotheses per participant per task: one correct, one wrong, each with test steps. The correct one came from the accepted Stack Overflow answer.
limits: The correct hypothesis came from the known answer, so this is an oracle list at 50% precision. A real generating tool would be worse. This does not test a generating tool.
agent_relevance: Matches our design if a model proposes a few candidates and code tests each. A short list with test steps was useful even at 50% precision.

source: Alaboudi and LaToza (2020) Using Hypotheses as a Debugging Aid
finding: Unaided developers rarely held a correct hypothesis. Correctness rose only in later stages, when they had more information and time.
numbers: 20 control-condition sessions. Stage 1: 27 hypotheses, 3 correct (11%). Stage 2: 35 total, 9 correct (25%). Stage 3: 15 correct (39%). About 2 hypotheses per defect.
limits: Stages added documentation and execution, so correctness gains mix time with new information. Correctness scored with a keyword rubric.
agent_relevance: Hypothesis quality is the scarce item. Generation should not stop at one or two candidates.

source: Alaboudi and LaToza (2020) Using Hypotheses as a Debugging Aid
finding: A correct hypothesis at stage two predicts fix success, however it was obtained. It is necessary-ish but not sufficient.
numbers: Logistic regression on 60 sessions: correct stage-two hypothesis gave about 5 times higher odds of fixing (p=0.01). 20 of 60 sessions failed; 6 of those 20 had the correct hypothesis but no working fix.
limits: Correlational inside the study. The six failures with a right hypothesis show a second barrier: turning the cause into a fix. One participant found the DOM-collection cause but edited an unrelated part.
agent_relevance: Two gates: right cause, then right edit. Test them separately (G3). A correct diagnosis is not a fix.

source: Alaboudi and LaToza (2020) Using Hypotheses as a Debugging Aid
finding: Showing likely fault locations did not help hypothesis formation or success. This is a negative result for fault localisation as an aid.
numbers: Locations group had correct hypotheses 45% (stage 2) and 60% (stage 3) vs control 45% and 75%. No effect on hypotheses (p=0.4125, p=0.1320) or on fixing (p=0.6710).
limits: Locations were simulated (one correct, one incorrect). Small N means low power. A null is not proof of no effect.
agent_relevance: A line number alone is weak. Give the agent a cause statement plus a test, and revise from real output (G2).

source: Alaboudi and LaToza (2020) Using Hypotheses as a Debugging Aid
finding: Potential hypotheses did not shorten time to fix and did not change time spent reading documentation. Participants wanted examples and code pointers.
numbers: No significant time difference (f=0.51, p=0.61). Successful participants spent 5% (control), 17% (locations), 6% (hypotheses) of time on documentation (f=1.7, p=0.19).
limits: The gain is in success rate, not speed. Few data points per cell for time to success.
agent_relevance: Expect the gain in pass rate at fixed budget, not in speed. Measure pass rate at equal tokens (G7).

source: Alaboudi and LaToza (2020) Using Hypotheses as a Debugging Aid
finding: Offering hypotheses was a stronger predictor of success than years of experience in the regression.
numbers: Controls: experience 0-20 years (median 2), technology knowledge 1-8 of 9 (median 4). Hypothesis condition was significant; years were not.
limits: Participants had low experience on average (median 2 years). The expertise effect was not tested well.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a larger model removes the hypothesis bottleneck. Expertise as a moderator is untested here.

source: Alaboudi and LaToza (2020) Using Hypotheses as a Debugging Aid
finding: A preliminary look at three live-streamed developers found missing or incorrect hypotheses made them stall, even with web search.
numbers: 3 videos of 177, 85 and 104 minutes. No rates in the text I read.
limits: Anecdotal. Three open-source projects. Streamers know they have an audience.
agent_relevance: Motivates an escape from a wrong hypothesis (S6). Gives no effect size.

source: Li and Coblenz (2026) A Grounded Theory of Debugging in Professional Software Engineering Practice
finding: Professionals did not state testable hypotheses. They held loose speculations and uncertainty, and sometimes deliberately did not test them at once, to avoid jumping to conclusions.
numbers: 7 professionals plus 5 streamers, 17 tasks. None of the developers articulated formal hypotheses.
quote: None of the developers articulated formal hypotheses
limits: Qualitative and small. No outcome comparison, so it cannot say whether formal hypotheses would help or hurt.
agent_relevance: A rival description of good practice: speculation as a background set plus structured tracing. It gives no performance contrast.

source: Li and Coblenz (2026) A Grounded Theory of Debugging in Professional Software Engineering Practice
finding: The authors note that interviews and personal accounts favour the scientific method, but observational studies and experiments support other strategies. They cite a 12-person study where stating and testing a hypothesis was rare.
numbers: Cited study: 79 fifteen-second instances of stating and testing a hypothesis vs 832 of source-code inspection (12 participants, one database performance bug).
limits: Second-hand number from their related work, not read in the original. One bug, one tool set.
agent_relevance: Self-report of method does not match behaviour. Do not trust a model's claim to have tested a hypothesis (G10).

source: Li and Coblenz (2026) A Grounded Theory of Debugging in Professional Software Engineering Practice
finding: Experience helped developers form hypotheses fast and skip information gathering. An experienced developer fixed a packaging bug that juniors had struggled with.
numbers: One case (P2). Mental-model work was about 57% of the time in the study (from the project summary; case not counted).
limits: Single anecdote on expertise. No matched comparison.
agent_relevance: Prior experience is a moderator. A retrieved similar-case memory may speed hypothesis forming. Test with a case library.

source: Parnin and Orso (2011) Are automated debugging techniques actually helping programmers?
finding: A ranked list of suspicious statements (Tarantula) helped only on the easy task and only for strong performers. It did not help on the harder task.
numbers: 34 participants in the first experiment, plus 10 new ones for the rank test. Tetris: mean 12:42 (tool) vs 14:14 (no tool), not significant in the final run. NanoXML: 20:16 vs 22:30, n.s. High performers (N=10), Tetris: 8:51 vs 14:28 (p<0.05).
limits: Graduate students, two-hour limit. A first run found a tool effect that did not appear in the final run. Small groups.
agent_relevance: Consistent with the Alaboudi null for fault locations. A ranked location list is a weak aid.

source: Parnin and Orso (2011) Are automated debugging techniques actually helping programmers?
finding: Moving the true fault from rank 7 to rank 35 did not change performance. Developers did not read the list in order.
numbers: Groups C and D (10 participants): same Tetris/NanoXML time ratio, 0.79. 37% of visits skipped more than one position (average skip 10). Average 10.3 direction changes per person (range 1 to 36).
limits: N=10 for the rank test, so low power. Participants also scanned for statements that fit their own hypothesis.
agent_relevance: Developers use a tool to confirm an existing hypothesis. A model given a ranked list may do the same, so require a test, not agreement.

source: Parnin and Orso (2011) Are automated debugging techniques actually helping programmers?
finding: Seeing the faulty line was not enough to know it was faulty. The assumption of perfect bug understanding fails.
numbers: Of 10 participants who clicked the faulty statement, 1 stopped using the tool. The rest spent on average 61% of their time (about 10 more minutes) still inspecting statements.
limits: 10 data points.
agent_relevance: Recognising a true cause is itself a failure point. Run a check on the candidate instead of trusting a read (G2, G3).

source: Parnin and Orso (2011) Are automated debugging techniques actually helping programmers?
finding: Some tool-free developers patched a symptom (changed the rotation code) rather than the root cause. No tool user did.
numbers: Several participants in traditional groups bypassed the failure; none in the tool groups (Tetris task). Exact counts not in the text I read.
limits: No counts. Observed, not tested.
agent_relevance: Proximate cause versus root cause: a passing test may hide a symptom fix.

source: Vessey (1985) Expertise in debugging computer programs: situation-based versus model-based problem solving
finding: Abstract-level finding from a search result: experts respond to the data in the task. Novices are constrained by preconceived ideas or early hypotheses about the source of error.
numbers: 16 programmers, verbal protocol analysis (search snippet). The PDF I fetched was a scan with no text layer, so I did not read it.
quote: experts respond to the data in the task while novices are constrained by preconceived ideas or early hypotheses
limits: Secondary abstract only. Expertise was defined by chunking ability, not years. Fixation was not measured as a rate.
agent_relevance: Candidate rule only: follow the data over the first idea. Not verified by me; do not cite as established.

source: Gould (1975) Some psychological evidence on how people debug computer programs
finding: Abstract-level: experienced programmers debugged 12 FORTRAN listings with one bug each. Assignment-statement bugs were about 3 times harder to find than array or interaction bugs.
numbers: 10 programmers, 12 listings, median time about 7 min, 11% of bugs not found, under 1 incorrect assertion about location per listing (search snippet only).
limits: Snippet only, not opened. Old language and setting. Debugging was about 3 times as efficient on programs debugged before.
agent_relevance: Bug type is a moderator of difficulty. Stratify any benchmark by bug type.

source: Katz and Anderson (1987) Debugging: an analysis of bug-location strategies
finding: Secondary summary only: goal-driven reasoning dominated when people debugged their own code. Data-driven hand simulation dominated for other people's code.
numbers: Lisp programmers, small 10-line programs (search snippet). Original not opened.
limits: Snippet only. Sources conflict on whether subjects were novices or experienced.
agent_relevance: Own-code versus other-code may be a moderator. An agent fixing its own code resembles the goal-driven case, with a risk of anchoring on its own intent.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation?
finding: At matched sample budget, repair after a failed test often barely beats drawing fresh samples. The gain depends on model and difficulty.
numbers: GPT-4 on APPS: 10 initial samples plus 1 repair each gave 1.05 times the pass@20 baseline; 2 samples plus 10 repairs each gave 0.97 times pass@22. GPT-4 on APPS gains up to 8%; GPT-3.5 only marginal.
limits: Python puzzles (HumanEval, APPS); Code Llama 13B, GPT-3.5, GPT-4; written feedback then repair, no debugger. Not a repository setting.
agent_relevance: Compare hypothesis-then-test loops with plain resampling at equal tokens (G7, G11).

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation?
finding: The bottleneck is the quality of the model's own diagnosis. Stronger-model feedback helped weaker models and human feedback helped GPT-4.
numbers: Replacing GPT-4's own explanation with a human one raised repair success from 33.3% to 52.6% (1.58 times). By difficulty: introductory 42.6 to 62.2, interview 19.3 to 45.7, competition 3.7 to 14.7. 16 participants, 2 feedbacks per program, 40 failing programs, 25 repair samples per feedback.
limits: Human feedback from 16 participants; time cost not measured; only 40 programs.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM analogue of Alaboudi: supplying a correct diagnosis is a large lever (about 1.6 times here) and it grows with difficulty.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation?
finding: GPT-4's own feedback was wrong far more often than human feedback.
numbers: Obviously inaccurate: 32 of 80 GPT-4 explanations vs 7 of 80 human ones.
limits: Judged at a cursory glance by the authors.
agent_relevance: Self-generated hypotheses fail often enough on hard items that a separate check must filter them.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Without oracle labels, asking a model to review and revise its own answer lowered accuracy. Earlier reported gains came from using the correct label to decide when to stop.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K: 75.9 standard, 75.1 after round 1, 74.7 after round 2. CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 and 41.8. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 and 89.0. With oracle label: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 84.3, GPT-4 97.5.
limits: Reasoning tasks, not code, and no execution feedback. It marks a boundary, not code repair itself.
agent_relevance: Confirms G2: revise only from an outside signal. Re-examining a hypothesis without new output tends to change correct answers to wrong ones.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Multi-agent debate was no better than self-consistency at an equal number of responses, per the introduction.
numbers: Stated in the introduction; I did not read the table.
limits: Only the summary statement checked.
agent_relevance: Matches G9.

source: Kang et al. (2023) Explainable Automated Debugging via Large Language Model-driven Scientific Debugging (AutoSD)
finding: A loop of hypothesis, prediction, experiment (debugger), observation and conclusion kept repair accuracy about equal to plain prompting while adding an explanation. It was not shown to beat plain sampling.
numbers: Compared with LLM-Base on Defects4J 1.2/2.0 and BugsInPy; 10 patches per bug. Text says the two are similar. About 5 times longer to produce a patch.
limits: No gain over the baseline at equal cost is claimed. Explanation is its main aim. ChatGPT-era model.
agent_relevance: A structured hypothesis loop is not a free accuracy win. It must pass the equal-compute test (G7).

source: Kang et al. (2023) Explainable Automated Debugging via Large Language Model-driven Scientific Debugging (AutoSD)
finding: Real execution results made the model's done signal more reliable. With model-imagined debugger output the signal flipped.
numbers: DONE token with real execution: 12.4 points more likely plausible. With simulated debugger output: 11 points less likely. Plausible patch in 73% of runs with the real debugger vs 63% without. Of bugs with a plausible patch, 89% correct when DONE was predicted vs 82% when not.
limits: Plausible is not correct. Correctness was hand-labelled on samples (100 patches for Defects4J).
agent_relevance: Direct support for G2 and G10: an imagined observation is worse than none. Code must supply observations.

source: Kang et al. (2023) Explainable Automated Debugging via Large Language Model-driven Scientific Debugging (AutoSD)
finding: Explanations helped human patch reviewers on real bugs. In one item reviewers accepted the model's reasoning without scrutiny and erred.
numbers: 20 participants (6 professionals), 12 patches, half shown with explanation. More accurate with explanation in 7 of 12 cases (5 on BugsInPy), less accurate in 2 (ARHE105, BIP003). Time about equal. 70% said explanations matter in repair tools.
limits: 12 items, tiny per-item counts, no overall significance test in the text I read.
agent_relevance: A fluent wrong hypothesis can persuade a judge. Do not show the explanation to a model judge (G5).

source: Kang et al. (2023) Explainable Automated Debugging via Large Language Model-driven Scientific Debugging (AutoSD)
finding: The loop mostly failed when the model chose a breakpoint that was never reached. The experiment failed, and the hypothesis ended undecided.
numbers: Example trace: breakpoint on an uncovered line gave 'hypothesis is undecided due to experiment error'. 25 failed cases examined.
limits: Qualitative, 25 cases.
agent_relevance: Give the scaffold an explicit undecided state, so a broken experiment does not count as refuting a hypothesis.

source: Levin, Van Kempen, Berger et al. (2025) ChatDBG: Augmenting Debugging with Large Language Models
finding: Giving the model debugger commands and a dialogue raised root-cause fixes. Extra features sometimes lowered success.
numbers: Python student programs, 10 runs each: plain 'why?' 57%, specialised queries 67%, with an extra dialog step 85%. C/C++ crashes: root cause fixed 36%, only the proximate cause fixed another 55%.
limits: Hand-judged, small program set. Authors say longer prompts can degrade the model in some configurations. No human-hypothesis comparison.
agent_relevance: Proximate versus root cause (55% vs 36%) is the LLM form of the symptom patch seen in Parnin and Orso.

source: Majgaonkar et al. (2025) Understanding Code Agent Behaviour: An Empirical Study of Success and Failure Trajectories
finding: Failed agent runs are longer and more spread out. Failing runs still find the right file, go wrong at fine-grained reasoning, and spend as long on wrong paths as on right ones.
numbers: OpenHands, SWE-agent, Prometheus on SWE-bench Lite and Verified. On Lite, failures took about 20 more steps (OpenHands, SWE-agent) and 49 more (Prometheus). On Verified 44, 22 and 74 more. Hunk-level localisation predicts success.
limits: Observational, three agents, trajectories coded by the authors. Not a causal test of hypotheses.
agent_relevance: Run length is a cheap trigger for the impasse state (G1). Time on wrong paths is how fixation looks in an agent.

source: Xiong (2026) Hypothesis generation and updating in large language models
finding: On a controlled number-game task, models lean toward narrow hypotheses by default. Prompting or thinking reduces this. Hypothesis generation and hypothesis evaluation gave different posteriors, so the probes are not interchangeable.
numbers: Eight non-thinking models (Gemma 4, Qwen 3.5/3.6, GPT-5.4 Mini, Nemotron 3 Nano). Models generalised poorly to an enlarged domain 1-200 after seeing 1-100.
limits: Toy task, not debugging, no execution check. I took the stated results only, not the figures.
agent_relevance: A model that ranks hypotheses and one that generates them can disagree. Prefer generate, then test in code.

source: Alaboudi and LaToza (2021) An Exploratory Study of Debugging Episodes
finding: Debugging time is dominated by a few long episodes, and no single activity explains the long ones. Self-inserted defects took 6 minutes against 51 for reported defects.
numbers: Sessions from 11 developers; 20 episodes and 166 activities coded, kappa 75% (episodes) and 84% (activities). Debugging was 48% of session time (range 13-95%). The 23 long episodes (about 32 min) made 80% of debugging time; the 23 short ones made 1%.
limits: Exploratory, two coders, sessions mixed. Hypotheses not measured directly.
agent_relevance: Time is heavy-tailed. Budget by difficulty (G12) and expect rare long stuck episodes.

source: Alaboudi and LaToza (2021) Edit-Run Behavior in Programming and Debugging
finding: Developers mostly test a guess by editing and running. They rarely inspect internal state or use automated tests.
numbers: 581 debugging edit-run cycles (207 programming). Median debugging cycle about 1 minute. Only 23% of run steps used logs or the debugger; 18% used automated tests. 94% of debugging cycles had no gaps. 70% edited one file. Text-editor users did 69% more cycles than IDE users.
limits: About 11 developers, small sample.
agent_relevance: Human tests are fast and look at final output. An agent can run many cycles, so the open question is whether more state-level observation helps.
